strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical analysis: the identification of 'Few-Patch Bias' using attention visualization, patch-masking experiments, and quantitative TDE-based patch attribution is a nice diagnostic contribution that is validated across several existing detectors (UnivFD, DRCT, Breaking).

Strong empirical results across two standard evaluation settings (GenImage/DRCT cross-generator generalization and the Chameleon sanity-check setting), with state-of-the-art average accuracy and notably lower variance across generative models (e.g., 97.2 mAcc with std 1.7 on GenImage).

Both proposed components (Random Patch Replacement and Patch-wise Contrastive Learning) are simple, easy to implement, and the ablation study (Table 4) cleanly shows each module contributes and their combination is significantly better than either alone (92.9 vs 97.2).
Robustness evaluations against JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, resizing, and random masking directly support the central claim that reducing over-reliance on a few patches improves robustness.
The paper positions itself well within the local vs. global detection taxonomy and discusses its relationship to patch-wise and CLIP-based methods.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Random Patch Replacement is a straightforward masking/pasting augmentation closely related to DRCT's diffusion-reconstruction strategy (in fact PPL builds directly on DRCT's reconstructed training pairs), and the margin-based patch-wise contrastive loss (Eq. 3) is a standard application of Hadsell et al. The core contribution is more an empirical finding plus augmentation recipe than a new technique.

The 'Lazy Learner' causal explanation for Few-Patch Bias is asserted rather than demonstrated; the paper shows the bias exists (correlationally via TDE) but provides no intervention that isolates curriculum/shortcut learning as the root cause.

Results on DRCT (mAcc ~99.5, std 0.1, with many subsets above 99.5%) appear near-saturated and raise questions about benchmark difficulty/leakage given the method is trained on diffusion-reconstructed pairs from the same distribution; the paper does not discuss this saturation.

Missing important hyperparameter details in the main text: replacement ratio r, number of patches m, margin α, loss weight λ, and sensitivity/ablations over these values are not reported, hurting reproducibility; no code release is mentioned.

Comparison fairness concerns: results are mixed across sources (some copied from C2P-CLIP, DRCT papers, some re-implemented, some taken from original papers), and backbone/training configurations differ between methods, making some rows hard to compare.

Several writing/presentation errors reduce polish: duplicated sentences in Section 3.1, a reference to 'Fig. 3' when Table 3 is meant, Table 3 caption typos ('an be sourced'), and the Chameleon claim of 'surpassing SOTA by 5%' is loosely stated relative to Table 3 numbers.

The theoretical claim that 'every patch contains synthetic artifacts' is essentially definitional for fully generated images and the supporting evidence (single-patch accuracy of 90%) conflates patch content discriminability with the desirability of using all patches; Chameleon results (~70%) also show a large remaining gap, which the framing underemphasizes.

strengths: The empirical analysis of 'Few-Patch Bias' using TDE-based counterfactual patch attribution is a reasonably novel and interesting diagnostic contribution, with both qualitative (attention maps, TDE heatmaps) and quantitative support (patch masking experiments)
The proposed PPL framework is simple, well-motivated relative to the analysis, and cheap to implement (patch replacement augmentation + patch-token contrastive loss)

Evaluation spans two standard settings (GenImage/DRCT cross-generator and Chameleon) with strong reported results, notably the lowest accuracy std across generators (1.7 on GenImage), and the paper includes ablations on both components and robustness studies to corruption and masking
The masking-robustness experiment provides direct evidence for the central claim that the method reduces reliance on specific patches
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Random Patch Replacement is essentially patch-level mixing of paired real/fake images (an extension of DRCT's reconstruction-based augmentation), and Patch-wise Contrastive Learning is a standard margin-based contrastive loss [6] applied to patch tokens; both are incremental on top of existing ideas

The core 'principles' (All Patches Matter, More Patches Better) are close to trivial for fully generated images — every pixel is synthetic by definition — so the conceptual contribution feels overclaimed; the paper also restricts to the fully-generated setting, so the claims do not extend to partial manipulation

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: many baseline results are copied from other papers [28, 1, 36] rather than re-run under identical conditions; the method itself uses diffusion-reconstructed paired data (following DRCT) while several baselines in Table 1 do not, which may confound the gains; only UnivFD was re-implemented with matched augmentations

The 18.7% accuracy drop from masking a single patch is presented as evidence of Few-Patch Bias, but masking a large region destroys real information content; this does not cleanly separate 'bias toward few patches' from ordinary sensitivity to occlusion

Some results are ambiguous: in Table 3 (All GenImage), the method's fake/real accuracy split (49.68/88.99) indicates a strong bias toward predicting real on Chameleon, weakening the generalization narrative; DRCT-benchmark accuracies are near-saturated (99.5), making differences less meaningful; no error bars or significance tests are reported
Restricting test images to 224x224 center crops at inference while training on random 224 crops may favor the patch-based method over baselines evaluated on full images

Several presentation issues undermine polish: 'Fig. 3 compares' should reference Table 3; inconsistent F3Net citation ([14] vs [22]); repeated sentences in Section 3.1; grammatical errors ('an be sourced'); DINOv2 variant shows noticeably weaker Chameleon balance (64.65/68.12)
No ablation on key hyperparameters (replacement ratio r, margin α, λ), and no analysis of how RPR/PCL interact with non-ViT backbones despite the method being framed as general

strengths: The paper provides an interesting diagnostic analysis of existing AIGI detectors, using attention maps, patch masking, and Total Direct Effect (TDE) to quantify and name a 'Few-Patch Bias' — this is a genuinely useful empirical observation for the community.

Comprehensive evaluation across two widely used settings (GenImage, DRCT cross-generator; Chameleon sanity check) with recent baselines (DRCT, Effort, SAFE, C2P-CLIP, Breaking), reporting both mAcc and standard deviation across generators.
The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art average accuracy with notably lower variance (e.g., 97.2 mAcc / std 1.7 on GenImage; 99.5 mAcc on DRCT), and ablations show both RPR and PCL contribute.
Robustness studies (JPEG compression, blur, resizing, random masking) support the claim that reduced patch over-reliance improves robustness.
The paper is generally well written and the motivation (artifact distribution is uniform across patches, so detectors should not shortcut to a few regions) is intuitive and clearly argued.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Random Patch Replacement is essentially a cutout/pasting-style augmentation and Patch-wise Contrastive Learning is a standard margin-based contrastive loss (Hadsell et al., 2006) applied to patch tokens. The contribution is mostly the empirical finding plus a straightforward combination of known techniques.

Potential evaluation confound: the authors follow DRCT and add diffusion-reconstructed images to training. On the DRCT benchmark the proposed method achieves near-uniform ~99.5% accuracy across all generator families. This could reflect learning the reconstruction process itself (as DRCT is designed to do) rather than the claimed patch-utilization mechanism, and it is not disentangled. The striking jump in the ablation (92.9 → 97.2 when combining RPR+PCL) is also unexplained and warrants deeper analysis.

Comparison fairness: most baseline numbers in Tables 1–3 are copied from other papers trained under different recipes, while the proposed method uses additional reconstructed training data and strong pre-trained backbones (CLIP, DINOv2) with LoRA. A controlled re-training of at least one strong baseline (e.g., DRCT or SAFE) with the same data and backbone is needed to isolate the benefit of PPL.

The TDE analysis has methodological issues: masking a patch to zero injects an out-of-distribution signal (real images contain no zero patches), so TDE values conflate patch importance with the artifact of zero-filling. Additionally, the claim 'more uniform TDE distribution → better generalization' is supported by only a few anecdotal examples (UnivFD vs. DRCT) rather than a systematic correlation analysis across many methods/detectors.

The 'All Patches Matter' evidence is weaker than claimed: the single-patch experiment (replicating one patch into a full image) creates highly unnatural repetitive textures that models may detect as anomalous, so 90% accuracy does not convincingly prove every patch individually carries discriminative artifacts. Figure 2 is qualitative.

Chameleon results reveal class-bias problems that are not discussed: Ours/CLIP gets 17.27% fake accuracy vs. 99.01% real accuracy under SD v1.4 training, which is near-worst-case behavior; the overall 63.94% is driven entirely by the real class. This undermines the generality claims on Setting-II.

Minor issues: some typos ('an be sourced', 'LORA'), reference inconsistencies (e.g., F3Net cited as both [22] and [14]), text references 'Fig. 3' where Table 3 is meant, and the claimed Chameleon result '70%, surpassing SOTA by 5%' is stated loosely without precise comparison conditions.

Reproducibility details (replacement ratio r, number of patches m, loss weight λ, margin α) are deferred to the appendix not included here; the sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters is not reported.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: the 'Few-Patch Bias' phenomenon is identified through multiple complementary pieces of evidence (attention maps, patch-occlusion fragility, and a quantitative CDE-based causal analysis), which is a genuinely interesting diagnostic contribution to the AIGI detection literature.

The proposed framework (Randomized Patch Reconstruction + Patch-wise Contrastive Learning) is simple, coherent, and directly tied to the diagnosed problem rather than being a loosely motivated engineering combination.

Evaluation is broad: experiments span GenImage, DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark, UniversalFakeDetect, and the in-the-wild Chameleon dataset, with comparisons against many recent strong baselines (DRCT, C2P-CLIP, Effort, SAFE, FatFormer, etc.), and consistent SoTA results with lower variance.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, p_rpr, r_rpr, s), loss choice (InfoNCE vs. margin-based), random vs. fixed-position reconstruction, patch size, and a comparison against random patch dropout; robustness under JPEG, blur, and resizing is also studied.
The appendix provides useful additional analyses (CDE distributions, Grad-CAM visualizations for both ViT and CNN backbones) that strengthen the 'Few-Patch Bias is model-agnostic' claim.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: RPR is closely related to DRCT's diffusion-reconstruction contrastive training, and the patch-wise contrastive loss is a standard margin-based contrastive objective (Hadsell et al., 2006). The contribution is largely a careful recombination of existing ideas guided by a new analysis; reviewers may view this as incremental.

Potential circularity/shortcut concern in evaluation: RPR uses SDv1.4 inpainting for reconstruction, and evaluation is heavily diffusion-centric (GenImage, DRCT-2M). The near-perfect DRCT-2M results (mAcc 99.50 ± 0.1, essentially 99+ on every subset) raise the question of whether the detector keys on SD-reconstruction artifacts rather than general synthetic cues. The paper does not convincingly disentangle this; a GAN-only training/evaluation experiment or reconstruction-model-vs-generator ablation would help.

Fairness of some comparisons is questionable: in Tables 3 and 4, PPL is trained on diffusion data (GenImage SDv1.4) while baselines are trained on GAN/ProGAN data. The paper acknowledges this in Table 3, but the resulting comparisons are difficult to interpret as head-to-head evidence.

The 'All Patches Matter / More Patches Better' principles are framed as formal contributions but are empirical observations rather than established principles; the causal 'Lazy Learner' attribution is asserted more than demonstrated (no direct intervention isolating the curriculum-effect mechanism).

Some experimental results are under-explained or anomalous, e.g., the non-monotonic behavior of patch dropout in Table 9 (0.15 gives 94.2 while 0.20 gives 89.1) is glossed over; also the relationship between Table 8's finding that larger patch sizes (28) outperform the default 14×14 on mAcc (97.6 vs. 97.2) contradicts the text's claim that the process 'is not sensitive to reconstruction patch size.'

Writing has noticeable rough edges (e.g., grammatical issues in the abstract such as 'We identify this bias to Lazy Learner effect, where detectors to limited patch artifacts'), and claims like 'All Patches Matter' are stated with more force than the evidence warrants, since a single patch reaching 90% accuracy is itself in tension with the necessity of using all patches.
No release of code/checkpoints is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the somewhat involved RPR pipeline and multiple tuned hyperparameters.

strengths: The paper evaluates on a broad suite of benchmarks (GenImage, DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark, UniversalFakeDetect, Chameleon) with many recent baselines, and reports ablations over hyperparameters, loss choices, and augmentation strategies.

The patch-wise contribution analysis (attention maps, patch masking, CDE-style logit deltas) is a reasonable empirical observation that detectors concentrate on few patches, and the visualization/appendix material is fairly thorough.

The overall idea of discouraging reliance on a few image regions is sensible and the proposed components (randomized patch reconstruction + patch-level contrastive loss) are simple and easy to reproduce.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of existing ideas — diffusion-reconstruction augmentation is the core of DRCT (explicitly cited and compared), and the margin-based contrastive loss is from Hadsell et al. (2006). The 'principles' (All Patches Matter / More Patches Better) are largely re-statements of known observations already exploited by patch-wise detectors (SSP, PatchCraft, etc.), packaged as if they were new findings.

The causal framing is superficial and technically shaky: computing logit differences after zeroing patches is standard occlusion/sensitivity analysis, not a credible 'Controlled Direct Effect'; the CDE notation is also inconsistent with 'TDE' used in the appendix, and the ad hoc exponential normalization of CDE values is unexplained and unjustified.

A significant confound threatens the validity of the headline results: training relies on SDv1.4 inpainting reconstruction, and several test sets (DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark diffusion subsets, GenImage SD subsets) contain artifacts from the same diffusion family. The jump from DRCT's 91.35 to 99.50 mAcc on DRCT-2M looks more like distribution alignment with the reconstruction model than genuine 'patch utilization' gains. On Tables 3–4 the baselines are deliberately trained on out-of-distribution GAN data while PPL is trained on diffusion data — the claimed advantage is partially built into the protocol.

Signs of carelessness undermine confidence: repeated rows/suspicious number duplication between Table 3 and Table 4 (the Ours/DINOv2 row in Table 4 repeats the Table 3 values for the GAN columns), broken Table 2 formatting, numerous grammatical errors ('we identify this bias to Lazy Learner effect, where detectors to limited patch artifacts', 'contributions are threefold', 'two vision foundation model as backbones'), and patch labels in the contrastive loss (patch_gt) never clearly defined for mixed real/synthetic images.

The lazy-learner/Few-Patch-Bias narrative is asserted rather than established: correlation between uniform attention/CDE and generalization is shown on a handful of examples and one comparison (DRCT vs UnivFD), with no controlled experiment demonstrating uniform patch usage is the cause of better generalization rather than a side effect.

In-the-wild results are weak (66–72% on Chameleon, far from practical) and the robustness section is thin (single figure, no baseline numbers in the text). No error bars/multiple seeds are reported for the main comparisons despite emphasizing low standard deviation across subsets as a selling point.

Strong claims in the title/abstract ('More Patches Better') are not rigorously validated: no systematic experiment varying the number of patches actually leveraged, and the ablation shows accuracy *degrades* at high reconstruction ratios, which partially contradicts the slogan.

strengths: The paper presents a clearly motivated analysis: the 'Few-Patch Bias' observation is supported by multiple lines of evidence (attention maps, patch masking experiments, and a quantitative CDE analysis), which is more rigorous than typical empirical-motivation sections.

The proposed PPL framework is simple and well-motivated, combining a data-level strategy (Randomized Patch Reconstruction) with a loss-level strategy (Patch-wise Contrastive Learning), and the two components are ablated both jointly and individually (Fig. 8, Tables 6-9).

Evaluation is broad: four major benchmarks (GenImage, DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark, UniversalFakeDetect) plus the in-the-wild Chameleon dataset, with comparisons against many recent strong baselines (UnivFD, FatFormer, DRCT, C2P-CLIP, Effort, SAFE, Breaking), and consistent reported gains in both accuracy and stability (lower std).

The appendix provides useful supplementary ablations (loss function choice, fixed vs. random patch placement, patch size, patch dropout alternative) and extensive qualitative CDE/Grad-CAM visualizations across generators and architectures (ViT and CNN), supporting the generality of the bias claim.
Robustness studies under JPEG compression, blur, and resizing are included, addressing a practical concern for real-world deployment.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core recipe is very close to DRCT (Chen et al., ICML 2024), which already combines diffusion-reconstruction-based data augmentation with contrastive training. The main delta is applying reconstruction/contrast at the patch level rather than the image level. The paper should more explicitly delineate its contribution from DRCT and ideally include an apples-to-apples patch-level vs. image-level comparison with DRCT under identical backbones and training budgets.

Potential train/test artifact leakage on DRCT-2M: the DR variants are produced by the same SD-based inpainting pipeline used for RPR training. Training the detector to spot SD-reconstruction traces could inflate the near-perfect DRCT-2M results (99.5 mAcc, ±0.1 std — a suspiciously large jump over DRCT's 91.35). The paper does not analyze or rule out this confound, and such uniformity across all subsets warrants scrutiny.

The CDE analysis has a methodological weakness: masking a patch by zero-filling introduces out-of-distribution inputs, so logit changes may reflect distribution shift rather than the patch's causal contribution to detection. A more careful intervention (e.g., noise infilling or reconstruction-based masking) or sensitivity analysis is needed.

Patch-level contrastive learning relies on patch ground-truth labels, but the paper does not clearly explain how patch labels are derived (presumably propagated from image labels). For real images this assumes all patches are artifact-free, and for RPR images the labels are correct by construction but may encourage the model to detect reconstruction traces rather than general generative artifacts.

Claims about 'uniform patch utilization' are supported mostly by qualitative heatmaps and violin plots; a quantitative metric for CDE uniformity with statistical tests, and a direct correlation between uniformity and generalization, would substantially strengthen the central claim.

Writing quality needs improvement: several grammatical errors and typos ('detectors to limited patch artifacts', 'we identify this bias to Lazy Learner effect', 'are threethfold', 'two vision foundation model'), inconsistent terminology, and some imprecise claims (e.g., asserting uniform artifact distribution as a property of 'modern generative models' without rigorous evidence across architectures such as autoregressive or discrete-token generators).

On Chameleon (the most realistic in-the-wild setting), absolute gains are modest (~66-72%), and the fake/real breakdown shows weak real-image recall for the SDv1.4-trained model (64.65/68.12), suggesting the method still struggles on genuine open-world data; this limitation is not discussed.

The framework inherits a practical dependency on an SD inpainting pipeline for training data construction; the computational and reproducibility implications (e.g., sensitivity to the choice of reconstruction model version) are only briefly addressed, and there is no analysis of how PPL behaves when the reconstruction generator differs significantly from test-time generators.
